public_rationale: Part of the claim holds. In late 2024 ChatGPT still hallucinated often. OpenAI's own table gives GPT-4o a 0.61 hallucination rate on SimpleQA. A November 2024 Tow Center audit found 153 wrong or partly wrong answers out of 200, with ChatGPT admitting uncertainty only seven times. So hallucinations did not fade into a minor problem. But the plain words 'They didn't [recede]' go too far. OpenAI reported that GPT-4 cut hallucinations sharply compared with GPT-3.5 in 2023, and that o1 hallucinated less than GPT-4o in 2024. Marcus concedes in the same post that hallucinations 'may have declined'. The result depends on which meaning of 'recede' is used.
limitations: The decline figures come from OpenAI's internal or self-built tests.
The Tow Center audit covers one task: attributing quotes to their sources.
Benchmarks differ across time, so there is no single trend line.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Despite projections by investors and tech companies, hallucinations and errors of misunderstanding in ChatGPT did not soon recede.

statement.excerpt: Labenz – and the countless venture capitalists and big tech companies that invested hundreds of billions in improving ChatGPT – projected that hallucinations and stupid errors of misunderstanding would soon recede.

from_speaker: hallucinations and stupid errors of misunderstanding
our_interpretation: The checkable part is 'They didn't': between early 2023 (Labenz's thread) and the post date, ChatGPT's hallucinations did not recede.

Two readings are possible. On a literal reading, 'recede' means 'measurably decline'. On a looser reading, it means 'fade into a minor problem'. In the same post Marcus writes 'They may have declined, but they certainly haven't vanished', which points to the second reading.
The claim about what Labenz and investors projected is framing and is not scored.
criteria.support_condition: Evidence that by late 2024 ChatGPT models still hallucinated often on standard factuality tests or in real use, and that rates did not fall over 2023–2024.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Evidence that ChatGPT's hallucination rates fell sharply between 2023 and late 2024, to the point where they were rare or minor.

evidence.excerpt: While still a real issue, GPT‑4 significantly reduces hallucinations relative to previous models (which have themselves been improving with each iteration).
evidence.explanation: OpenAI reported a measurable drop in hallucinations from GPT-3.5 to GPT-4 in early 2023. This goes against a literal reading that hallucinations did not recede at all.

evidence.excerpt: According to these evaluations, o1‑preview and o1 hallucinate less frequently than GPT‑4o, and o1‑mini hallucinates less frequently than GPT‑4o‑mini.
evidence.locator: section Hallucination evaluations, text after Table 3
evidence.explanation: Newer OpenAI models hallucinated less than GPT-4o on OpenAI's own tests, so rates kept falling in 2024. The same Table 3 still shows hallucination rates of 0.61 for GPT-4o and 0.44 for o1-preview on SimpleQA.

evidence.excerpt: In total, ChatGPT returned partially or entirely incorrect responses on a hundred and fifty-three occasions, though it only acknowledged an inability to accurately respond to a query seven times.
evidence.explanation: In November 2024 an independent audit found ChatGPT gave wrong or partly wrong source answers 153 times out of 200, and rarely said it was unsure. So fabrication was still common two years after launch.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: A consistent independent benchmark measuring ChatGPT hallucination rates from 2023 to late 2024, along with an agreed meaning of 'recede'.
